opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find really distinctive about K–12 is that you can't just take the frameworks we've built for adults and transplant them. A lot of the conversation around acceptable use of language models assumes a user who's an autonomous adult, someone who can consent, who has a fairly developed sense of when to trust a source and when to be skeptical. With kids, none of those assumptions hold cleanly, and they shift a lot between a second grader and a high school senior.

The second thing is that education has a goal beyond task completion. In most settings, if the model helps you get the answer faster, that's a win. In a classroom, getting the answer is often beside the point; the point is the student building the skill. So "acceptable use" becomes much more about whether a use supports or undermines learning, and that's a harder thing to measure. The same interaction, say, having a model draft an essay outline, could be a great scaffold for one student and a crutch for another.

Third, there are so many stakeholders. You've got students, teachers, parents, administrators, district policy, state requirements, and they don't always agree. Teachers in particular are being asked to make these calls on the fly, often without much support or evidence about what actually works. So part of what I think about is how we, as researchers, can give them better tools, both evaluation methods that reflect educational values and clearer guidance, rather than leaving every teacher to reinvent policy in their own classroom.

And finally, the stakes around safety and privacy are just elevated. Kids' data, exposure to inappropriate content, the potential for a model to confidently say something wrong to someone who isn't equipped to catch it: these aren't edge cases in K–12, they're central design concerns. So it really pushes you to think about evaluation and governance in a more context-specific way, which I think is actually a healthy lesson for the field more broadly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one I find really interesting, because K–12 education is a setting where the usual framing of "is this output harmful or not" kind of breaks down. A lot of the way we evaluate language models today is built around this idea that there's some property of the output itself that makes it acceptable or unacceptable. Is it toxic, is it factually wrong, does it leak private information. And in education, that framing just isn't sufficient, because the same output can be totally fine in one context and genuinely problematic in another.

The example I like to use is something like a student asking a model to write an essay. If you're a professional writer, having a model draft something for you is a productivity tool, nobody blinks. If you're a tenth grader whose assignment is specifically about learning to construct an argument, the exact same output undermines the whole point of the exercise. The text is identical. What changed is the purpose, the stakeholder, and what the interaction is supposed to accomplish. So acceptability here is really a property of the use, not the content, and most of our evaluation infrastructure isn't set up to reason about that.

The second thing that's distinctive is that you have this very layered set of stakeholders who don't necessarily agree. You have the student, the teacher, the parents, the school district, and then you have policy at the state or national level. And these groups have different and sometimes conflicting ideas about what the technology is for. A teacher might care most about whether the tool supports learning versus shortcuts it. A parent might be primarily worried about safety or data privacy. An administrator might be thinking about equity and whether access is uniform across classrooms. So when we talk about determining acceptable use, there isn't a single ground truth you can just measure against. It's really a question of whose values get encoded, and how you surface those tradeoffs rather than quietly baking one group's preferences into the system.

And then the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that we're talking about minors whose capabilities are still developing. With adults, you can lean on the idea that the user has some judgment about when to trust the system and when not to. With a nine-year-old, that assumption doesn't hold in the same way. So things like sycophancy, or a model confidently asserting something wrong, have a different weight. The harms are also developmental and longitudinal, they show up over years rather than in a single interaction, which makes them really hard to study with the kinds of benchmarks we typically build.

So from my side as someone who works on evaluation and trustworthy ML, what this pushes me toward is thinking about context-dependent evaluation. Not "is this model safe," but "is this model appropriate for this task, for this population, under these norms." That's a much harder measurement problem, but I think it's the honest version of the question, and education is one of the clearest places where you can't avoid confronting it.

astra-6.text:
What makes K–12 education distinctive is that deciding what’s acceptable isn’t just a technical question. It’s a question about what we want students to learn, and who gets to make that decision. Teachers, parents, students, and school districts may have different expectations, and the appropriate use can change with the age of the student and the purpose of the assignment.

For example, getting help rewriting a paragraph might be useful if you’re trying to understand a science concept. But if the assignment is meant to develop your writing skills, that same assistance could bypass the thing you’re supposed to practice. So it’s hard to draw a universal line around an acceptable use. You have to connect it to the learning objective and ask whether the model is helping the student develop that ability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s distinctive is that the goal isn’t simply to get the right answer. It’s to help a student develop the ability to get there. A language model might produce a great essay or solve a math problem, but whether that’s useful depends on what the student is supposed to be learning. The same tool could support learning by offering feedback or undermine it by doing the work for them.

And K–12 covers a huge range of ages and developmental stages. What’s appropriate for a high school senior may be very different from what’s appropriate for a young child. Students also have less ability to assess when a model is wrong or when they should question it.

So I see this as a question that needs educators, parents, and students involved, alongside the people building the technology. We need to ask what learning objective a particular use serves, what oversight is needed, and how we’ll know whether it actually helps.
